A.explanation: Charge passing a point per unit time is the current $I$, which is the same everywhere in a series circuit so it cannot be less in one wire.

B.explanation: From $I = nAvq$, the larger cross-sectional area $A$ of the thick wire needs a smaller drift speed $v$ to carry the same current $I$.

C.explanation: Number density $n$ depends on the material, and both wires are copper, so $n$ is essentially the same in both wires.

D.explanation: The number of electrons per unit time is $I/e$, and since $I$ is the same in series, this rate is the same in both wires.

hints: Notice the thick wire and thin wire are in series with the cell, so the current $I$ - charge per unit time - must be identical in both.
Recall the drift-speed relation $I = nAvq$, where $n$ is number density, $A$ is cross-sectional area and $v$ is drift speed.
Both wires are copper so $n$ is the same, but $A$ is much larger for the thick wire - decide what this forces $v$ to do to keep $I$ constant.
walkthrough: The diagram shows one loop with the cell, thick wire and thin wire all in series, so the current $I$ is the same in both wires.
Use the microscopic current equation $I = nAvq$, where $n$ is the number density of free electrons, $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $v$ is the mean drift speed and $q = e$ is the electron charge.
Both wires are copper, so the material property $n$ is the same, and $q$ is a constant, while $I$ is fixed by the series connection.
Rearranged, $v = I/(nAq)$, so for fixed $I$, $n$ and $q$, drift speed is inversely proportional to area: $v$ is proportional to $1/A$.
The thick wire has significantly larger $A$ than the thin wire, so its electrons can drift much more slowly and still deliver the same charge per unit time.
